title: TCP Friendly Rate Control (TFRC): Protocol Specification
summary: Specifies TCP Friendly Rate Control, a congestion control mechanism for unicast flows in best-effort networks. It is reasonably fair when competing with TCP flows but varies throughput much less over time, which suits streaming media where a smooth sending rate matters. It replaced RFC 3448.

eli5.summary: TCP speeds up and slows down in jerky bursts. This way of sharing the road is just as polite to other drivers but cruises more steadily, which is nicer for video and calls.

questions: how does tfrc differ from tcp congestion control
what is the tcp throughput equation
subtitle: A congestion control mechanism that shares bandwidth fairly with TCP but changes its sending rate much more smoothly.

tldr.problem: TCP halves its sending rate after a single packet drop, which makes throughput jumpy and a poor fit for telephony or streaming media that want a steady rate.
tldr.mechanism: The receiver measures the loss event rate and reports it. The sender measures round-trip time, feeds both into the TCP throughput equation, and caps the result at twice the receive rate to get its allowed sending rate.
tldr.outcome: TFRC stays reasonably fair to TCP, meaning within a factor of two of a TCP flow's rate, with much lower variation, but it reacts more slowly to changes in available bandwidth. RFC 5348 obsoletes RFC 3448.

today: RFC 5348 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3448 and updates RFC 4342; no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. It tells DCCP CCID 3 and CCID 4 implementations to use it instead of RFC 3448 as the specification of TFRC.

sections.title: What TFRC Is For
sections.content:
TCP Friendly Rate Control (TFRC) is a congestion control mechanism for unicast flows in a best-effort Internet that compete with TCP traffic. It is not a complete protocol. It does not define packet formats or reliability, and is meant to be used inside a transport protocol such as DCCP, in an application that does its own end-to-end congestion control, or in endpoint congestion management.

The RFC calls a flow reasonably fair if its sending rate is generally within a factor of two of the rate of a TCP flow under the same conditions. TFRC meets that goal while varying its throughput far less than TCP does, which suits applications such as telephony or streaming media.

The price is a slower response to changes in available bandwidth. The RFC says TFRC should only be used when an application needs smooth throughput. For applications that simply want to move as much data as fast as possible, it recommends TCP, or an AIMD scheme with TCP-like parameters if reliability is not needed.
sections.eli5: TFRC is a rule for how fast to send data so you share the road fairly with TCP, but without the sudden slowdowns. It is best when you want a steady stream, like a video call.

sections.title: The Core Mechanism and Throughput Equation
sections.content:
TFRC works in a loop. The receiver measures the loss event rate and feeds it back to the sender. The sender also uses the feedback messages to measure round-trip time (RTT). It puts both into a throughput equation, and the resulting rate is limited to at most twice the receive rate to give the allowed transmit rate X. The sender then adjusts to match X.

A loss event is one or more lost or ECN-marked packets from a window of data. The equation currently required is a slightly simplified version of the Reno TCP equation from [PFTK98]. Its inputs are the segment size s, the round-trip time R, the loss event rate p (between 0 and 1.0), the TCP retransmission timeout t_RTO and the number of packets acknowledged by one TCP acknowledgement, b.

Implementations SHOULD set t_RTO = 4*R, and the use of b = 1 is RECOMMENDED. With those choices the equation simplifies to X_Bps = s / (R * (sqrt(2*p/3) + 12*sqrt(3*p/8)*p*(1+32*p^2))). Later updates could substitute a different equation, provided it reasonably approximates TCP's sending rate.
sections.eli5: There is a formula that says how fast a polite TCP sender would go, given how often packets get lost and how long a round trip takes. TFRC just plugs in those two numbers and sends at that speed.

sections.title: The Data Sender
sections.content:
Each data packet carries a sequence number that MUST increase by one per packet, a timestamp, and the sender's current RTT estimate. Each feedback packet from the receiver carries the timestamp of the last data packet received, the time elapsed at the receiver (t_delay), the measured receive rate X_recv, and the receiver's loss event rate p.

When feedback arrives the sender MUST compute an RTT sample, R_sample = (t_now - t_recvdata) - t_delay, and smooth it with R = q*R + (1-q)*R_sample, where a q of 0.9 is RECOMMENDED. It then updates the allowed rate. While p is zero the sender is in an initial slow-start and can roughly double its rate each round trip. Once p is above zero, X = max(min(X_Bps, recv_limit), s/t_mbi), where recv_limit is twice the largest recent receive rate and t_mbi is a maximum backoff interval of 64 seconds, so at least one packet is allowed every 64 seconds.

If the sender gets no feedback for four round-trip times, a nofeedback timer expires and the sender cuts its allowed rate in half. The timer starts at two seconds before the first RTT sample. A sender that has been idle is not cut below a recover rate equal to its initial rate. The initial rate is W_init/R with W_init = min(4*MSS, max(2*MSS, 4380)).

The sender also keeps a small set of recent receive rates and treats data-limited intervals, where it was not sending as much as allowed, specially so that a quiet application is not penalised for a low measured receive rate. To limit bursts after idle periods, an implementation MUST prevent bursts of arbitrary size, and the limit MUST be no more than one round-trip time's worth of packets. Reducing oscillations by scaling the rate with the square root of the RTT is RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: The sender keeps checking how long a round trip takes and what the receiver says about lost packets, then picks a speed. If it hears nothing for a while, it assumes trouble and slows to half speed.

sections.title: Measuring the Loss Event Rate
sections.content:
The receiver does the loss measurement. A packet is considered lost when at least NDUPACK packets with higher sequence numbers have arrived, with NDUPACK set to 3, as in TCP. A late packet can still fill the hole and the loss event rate is recalculated. For an ECN-capable connection, a marked packet counts as a congestion event as soon as it arrives. A retransmission is REQUIRED to get a new sequence number rather than reusing the lost packet's.

Losses are grouped into loss events using the RTT: if a new lost packet's estimated arrival time is within one RTT of the one that started the previous loss event, it belongs to the same event. The sequence space is then divided into loss intervals.

The receiver averages the most recent n intervals with weights that give full weight to the newer half and linearly decreasing weight to older ones. Setting n to 8 is RECOMMENDED, which gives weights 1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.8, 0.6, 0.4, 0.2. TFRC SHOULD NOT use values of n greater than 8 for traffic that might compete with TCP in the global Internet. The loss event rate is then p = 1 / I_mean. The current interval is included only if it is long enough to raise the average.

An OPTIONAL history discounting mechanism lets the receiver put more weight on a very long current interval, so TFRC responds a bit faster to the sudden absence of congestion. Its lower bound THRESHOLD is recommended to be 0.25.
sections.eli5: The receiver keeps a scorecard of how many packets passed between each time something got lost. Longer gaps mean a healthier road. It averages the recent gaps, with newer ones counting more, to decide how bumpy things are.

sections.title: The Data Receiver
sections.content:
The receiver sends feedback at least once per RTT. If the sender is sending less than one packet per RTT, the receiver sends a feedback packet for every data packet. It SHOULD also send feedback immediately when a new loss event is detected, and when an out-of-order packet removes a loss event from its history.

Each feedback report contains the measured receive rate over the previous round trip, the current loss event rate, and the echoed timestamp information. If no data packets have arrived since the last report, no feedback is sent.

When the first data packet arrives, the receiver sets p and X_recv to 0, sends a feedback packet, and starts the feedback timer. After the first loss event, the receiver MUST seed its loss history with a synthetic loss interval, found by choosing the p for which the throughput equation yields a rate within 5% of the target rate, taken as the maximum X_recv seen so far. If the very first packet is lost or marked, the target is 0.5 packets per RTT.

The document also describes sender-based variants, in which the receiver reliably reports losses and the sender computes the rate. DCCP's CCID 3 can be used as one. The advantage is that the sender need not trust the receiver's loss calculation.
sections.eli5: The receiver sends a short report back about once per round trip, and sends one right away if something just went wrong. The very first report is a special case, because there is no history yet.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
TFRC is a congestion control mechanism, not a transport protocol, so security must mostly be handled by the transport protocol that uses it. Congestion control can be abused for denial of service through spoofed feedback, so any such protocol should accept feedback only from the receiver of the data.

A greedy receiver could also claim to have received packets that were actually lost, to get more than its fair share of bandwidth. Defences normally involve a nonce that the receiver must echo, whose details depend on the transport protocol. The RFC expects protocols that combine ECN with TFRC to use the ECN nonce from [RFC3540], and points to the sender-verification discussions in RFC 4342 for use in DCCP.
sections.eli5: A sneaky receiver could lie about what it got so the sender sends faster than is fair. Protocols using TFRC need ways to check the receiver is telling the truth.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 3448
sections.content:
The main change is a set of mechanisms for senders that are data-limited, meaning they are not sending as much as allowed. The RFC also lets a sender accumulate up to a round-trip time of unused send credits and so send a burst after a quiet period.

Other changes: the initial sending rate can be as high as four packets per round-trip time, following RFC 3390, where RFC 3448 used two. A coarse-grained timestamp that increments every quarter of a round-trip time is allowed, following RFC 4342. The nofeedback rule is clarified: the sender halves its rate after four round-trip times without feedback, fixing contradictory text in RFC 3448 about two versus four. The history discounting THRESHOLD changed from 0.5 to 0.25. Handling of a lost first packet, slow-start corner cases and the RFC 3448 errata were also incorporated.
sections.eli5: This update fixes small mistakes in the older version, allows a faster start, and teaches the sender what to do when the application simply has nothing to send for a while.
